title: See-through, blurry or blocked: transparent, translucent and opaque

summary.text: This unit is about what happens when light meets a material. A transparent material, like window glass, lets light straight through, so you can see clearly through it. A translucent material, like butter paper, lets light through but jumbles it, so you see a glow but no clear picture. An opaque material, like a steel plate, lets no light through. We choose each kind for a job: glass for windows, thin curtains for soft light, thick curtains for sleep, and sunglasses to let in only part of the light. Being see-through is not fixed. It changes with thickness, with oil or water in the gaps, and even with which side is brighter. Your own hand lets red light through, and the whole universe was once a glowing fog that light could not cross.
summary.art: Three windows side by side: clear glass showing a sharp neem tree, frosted glass showing only a green glow, and a wooden shutter showing nothing, with a child's hand glowing red over a torch in the corner.

intro.hook: Go into a dark room with a torch. Press the torch against the tips of your fingers and switch it on. What colour do your fingers glow?
intro.text: Your fingers glow red. So some light is going right through your hand! We usually think a hand is something you cannot see through. But light does get through, a little. It just gets so jumbled on the way that no picture comes out. This unit is about three kinds of materials. Some let light straight through. Some let it through but jumble it. Some stop it. You will find out which is which, why, and how people use each kind every day.
intro.art: A child in a dark room pressing a torch under their fingertips, the fingers glowing a warm red with dark lines where the bones are.

outcomes: I can say what transparent, translucent and opaque mean, and sort real things into the three groups by testing them with light.
I can run a fair test to compare how see-through materials are, measure with a ruler, and show my results in a table and a bar chart.
I can explain that translucent things blur light because it bounces off many tiny edges inside them, and that filling the gaps with oil or water makes them clearer.
I can choose the right material for a job, like windows, curtains, sunglasses, lanterns and food containers, and say why.
I can explain that being see-through is not fixed. It depends on the thickness, the kind of light and which side is brighter.
I can say what scientists agree about see-through materials, and what they still do not know, like what glass really is.
I can give big examples: my glowing hand, see-through glass frogs, light that takes thousands of years to escape the Sun, and the universe that was once a fog.

terms.meaning: Light is what lets us see. It comes from things like the Sun, a bulb or a flame, and travels out from them.
terms.example: Sunlight comes in through the window in the morning.
terms.art: Sunbeams coming through a window onto a kitchen floor.

terms.meaning: A material is what a thing is made of.
terms.example: A window is made of glass. A curtain is made of cloth.
terms.art: A window, a curtain and a steel plate with labels: glass, cloth, steel.

terms.meaning: A transparent material lets light go straight through. You can see clearly through it.
terms.example: Window glass, clean water and cling film are transparent.
terms.art: A child looking through a clear glass window at a sharp neem tree outside.

terms.meaning: A translucent material lets light through, but jumbles it. You see a glow or blurry shapes, but not a clear picture.
terms.example: Butter paper, a frosted bathroom window and a thin white dupatta are translucent.
terms.art: A torch shining through butter paper, making a soft round glow on the wall.

terms.meaning: An opaque material does not let light through. You cannot see anything through it.
terms.example: A wooden door, a steel plate and a brick wall are opaque.
terms.art: A torch shining on a steel plate, with a dark shadow behind it.

terms.meaning: To scatter light is to send it bouncing off in many directions, like a ball hitting lots of pillars.
terms.example: Frosted glass scatters light, so you see only a blur through it.
terms.art: Little arrows of light entering a frosted pane and bouncing out in every direction.

terms.meaning: To absorb light is to soak it up. The light's energy stays in the material and warms it.
terms.example: A black umbrella absorbs sunlight and gets hot.
terms.art: A black umbrella in the sun with wavy heat lines rising from it.

terms.meaning: A shadow is a dark patch where light has been blocked.
terms.example: An opaque steel plate makes a dark shadow. Butter paper makes only a pale shadow.
terms.art: Two shadows on a wall, one dark from a plate and one pale from butter paper.

terms.meaning: Frosted glass is glass with a rough surface. The roughness scatters light, so the glass is translucent.
terms.example: Many bathroom windows have frosted glass. Light comes in, but nobody can see in.
terms.art: A bathroom window of frosted glass, glowing, with a blurry plant behind it.

terms.meaning: A tinted material is see-through but darkened, so less light gets through.
terms.example: Sunglasses and some car windows are tinted.
terms.art: A pair of dark sunglasses with the world behind them looking dimmer.

terms.meaning: Ultraviolet light is light from the Sun that our eyes cannot see. Too much of it burns skin and can harm eyes.
terms.example: Good sunglasses are marked 'UV400'. That means they block ultraviolet light.
terms.art: Sunglasses with a small 'UV400' sticker on one lens.

terms.meaning: Glare is light so bright that it is hard to see properly.
terms.example: Sunlight on a white wall or on water can cause glare.
terms.art: A child squinting at a bright white wall in the midday sun.

terms.meaning: A jaali is a screen of stone, wood or metal with holes cut in a pattern. The solid parts block light and the holes let it in.
terms.example: Old forts, mosques and tombs in India have carved stone jaalis.
terms.art: A carved stone jaali with sunlight making a pattern of bright spots on the floor.

terms.meaning: A fair test changes only one thing at a time, and keeps everything else the same.
terms.example: In the gap test, we change only the material. The letters, the light and the ruler stay the same.
terms.art: Five strips of material in a row next to the same card of big letters and a ruler.

terms.meaning: A molecule is a tiny group of atoms joined together. Atoms are the tiny pieces everything is made of.
terms.example: Water is made of water molecules, far too small to see.
terms.art: A drop of water with a zoomed-in circle showing tiny linked balls.

explanations.concept: Three things light can do when it meets a material
explanations.definition: When light meets a material, it can go straight through, it can be scattered in all directions, or it can be stopped by being absorbed or sent back.
explanations.description: Light always does something when it reaches a material. If most of it goes straight through, the material is transparent. If it goes through but is bounced about on the way, the material is translucent. If none of it gets through, the material is opaque. Most materials do a bit of each. We name them by what they mostly do.
examples: Window glass sends most light straight through.
Butter paper lets light through, but scatters it.
A steel plate lets none through. It sends some back and absorbs the rest.
explanations.art: Three panels: light arrows going straight through glass, zigzagging through butter paper, and stopping at a steel plate.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what light can do when it meets a material.

explanations.definition: A transparent material lets light pass straight through without jumbling it, so you can see a clear picture through it.
explanations.description: Look out of a clean window. The light from the tree outside comes through the glass in straight lines, all in order. So the picture of the tree stays sharp. Transparent does not mean invisible. You can still see a glass of water on the table. That is because a little light bounces off its surfaces, and its edges bend the light a little.
examples: Window glass, spectacle lenses and a clear plastic bottle are transparent.
Air is transparent. That is why you can see across a whole cricket ground.
Clean water in a steel tumbler is transparent. You can see the bottom of the tumbler.
explanations.art: A child looking through a window at a sharp tree, with straight light lines from the tree passing through the glass to the eye.
explanations.context: This card is about transparent materials, the ones you can see clearly through.

explanations.concept: Translucent: light gets through, but jumbled
explanations.definition: A translucent material lets light through but scatters it on the way, so you see a glow or blurry shapes but no clear picture.
explanations.description: Inside butter paper there are millions of tiny paper threads with air between them. Each time light goes from air into a thread, or back out, some of it changes direction. After thousands of these little turns, the light comes out in every direction. The light still gets through, but the picture is lost. Here is a surprise. If the paper touches a page of writing, you can read it. Lift the paper a little and the words blur away. The light from each letter spreads out more, the further it has to travel after the paper.
examples: A frosted bathroom window lets light in but hides you.
A thin cotton dupatta lets light through, so a room behind it glows.
A paper lantern glows all over, but you cannot see the bulb inside.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in drawing of butter paper as a tangle of threads, with a light arrow bouncing between them and coming out in many directions.
explanations.context: This card is about translucent materials, the ones that let light through but not a clear picture.

explanations.definition: An opaque material does not let light through. It absorbs the light, sends it back, or both.
explanations.description: A wooden door is opaque. Light that hits it is partly absorbed, and partly sent back into the room. None comes out of the other side. That is why an opaque thing makes a dark shadow behind it. Black things absorb most of the light that falls on them, so they warm up in the sun. Shiny metal sends most light back, which is why a steel plate gleams.
examples: A brick wall, a wooden almirah and a steel plate are opaque.
A thick blackout curtain is opaque, so a room can be dark in the afternoon.
A black umbrella is opaque and absorbs sunlight. Its cloth gets hot.
explanations.art: A torch beam hitting a wooden door, with a few arrows bouncing back and the rest fading into the wood, and darkness behind.
explanations.context: This card is about opaque materials, the ones that do not let light through.

explanations.concept: Many tiny edges make things cloudy
explanations.definition: A material looks cloudy or white when light bounces off many tiny edges inside it. Fewer edges make it clearer.
explanations.description: One big clear crystal of sugar is quite see-through. A pile of sugar grains is white, because light bounces off every grain's edges. Stir the sugar into water and it vanishes. The water is clear again, because the sugar has broken into molecules far too small to bounce light. The same is true for ice and snow. A clear ice cube is transparent. Crushed ice and snow are white, because of all their edges. Bubbles trapped in ice make it cloudy too. Oil on paper fills the air gaps between the threads. Then light passes from thread to oil without bouncing much, so the paper turns see-through.
examples: Foam on top of water is white, though the water and the air are both clear.
A spot of oil from a pakora makes the newspaper see-through.
A wet white T-shirt is more see-through than a dry one.
explanations.art: Three bowls: a pile of white sugar, a spoon stirring it into water, and a clear glass of sugar water with sparkles fading.
explanations.context: This card explains why some things are cloudy or white even when they are made of clear stuff.

explanations.concept: Why glass is see-through but metal is not
explanations.definition: Light is made of tiny packets of energy. Glass lets light through because its atoms cannot soak up the packets of light we see. Metal stops light because it has loose electrons that catch the light and send it back.
explanations.description: Every atom has electrons, tiny parts that move around its middle. An electron can only soak up a packet of light if the packet has just the right amount of energy for it. In glass, the electrons need a much bigger packet than the light we see carries. So the light just passes by, like a small coin that does not fit a big slot. Metals are different. Some of their electrons are loose and free to move. They catch the light easily and throw it back. That is why metals are opaque and shiny. This is a simple way of telling a story from quantum physics, the science of very tiny things.
examples: Clear glass lets the light we see through, but stops much of the Sun's ultraviolet light, which has bigger packets.
A steel plate is opaque and shiny because of its loose electrons.
Gold beaten very thin, called gold leaf, lets a little greenish light through.
explanations.art: A row of glass atoms like slots too big for small light coins, which roll past, beside a metal with loose electrons catching and throwing back light.
explanations.context: This card zooms in to the atoms, to explain why glass is see-through and metal is not.

explanations.concept: See-through depends on the kind of light
explanations.definition: A material can be transparent to one kind of light and opaque to another.
explanations.description: Our eyes see only some kinds of light. There are other kinds we cannot see. Window glass lets the light we see through, but blocks much of the ultraviolet light that gives sunburn. Your hand stops most light, but lets red light through, which is why your fingers glow red over a torch. A brick wall is opaque to light, yet radio signals and Wi-Fi go through it. So 'transparent' always means transparent to some kind of light.
examples: Your fingertips glow red over a torch, because red light gets through skin and blood best.
A phone gets signals inside a brick house.
Doctors use X-rays, another invisible light, to see bones through skin.
explanations.art: A brick wall with sunlight bouncing off it while wavy radio waves pass right through to a phone inside.
explanations.context: This card is about a surprise: whether something is see-through depends on which kind of light is shining on it.

explanations.definition: Through a thin curtain or net, you can see from the darker side into the brighter side, but not the other way.
explanations.description: A thin curtain lets a little light through each way. In the daytime the street is much brighter than your room. Lots of light comes in from the street, so you can see out. Only a little light goes out from your dim room, and it is swamped by the bright light bouncing off the curtain. So people outside see only a bright cloth. At night it flips. Your lamp makes the room the bright side. Now people outside can see in, and you see only the curtain. Many families add a thick, opaque curtain for the night.
examples: In the day, a thin net curtain hides you. At night with the lights on, it does not.
A shadow-puppet show uses a translucent screen with a lamp behind it, so the audience sees the shapes.
A car with tinted windows is easy to see into at night if its lights are on inside.
explanations.art: Two pictures of the same window with a thin curtain: by day a girl inside is hidden and the street is bright; by night her lamp is on and her shape shows to the street.
explanations.context: This card explains why a thin curtain hides you in the day but not at night.

explanations.concept: Using the three kinds: windows, curtains and sunglasses
explanations.definition: People choose transparent, translucent or opaque materials depending on whether they want to see through, to let light in privately, or to block light.
explanations.description: Windows are transparent, so we can see out and let sunlight in. Bathroom windows are often translucent, so light comes in but nobody can see in. Thin curtains soften bright light. Thick curtains are opaque, so a baby can sleep in the afternoon. Sunglasses are tinted. They let only part of the light through, so bright sunshine is less dazzling. Good sunglasses also block ultraviolet light. Never look at the Sun, even with sunglasses. They do not make it safe.
examples: Milk and medicine often come in opaque or dark bottles, because light can spoil them.
A paper lantern, called a kandil, makes a bulb's light soft and spread out.
A stone jaali lets light and air in but keeps a room private and cool.
explanations.art: A house cut in half showing a clear window, a frosted bathroom window, a thick bedroom curtain, a kandil lantern, and a child in sunglasses on the balcony.
explanations.context: This card is about how people use transparent, translucent and opaque materials in daily life.

explanations.definition: Some animals are almost transparent. This helps them hide, because predators look straight through them.
explanations.description: Being see-through is a clever way to hide. Many jellyfish are almost all water, so they are nearly invisible in the sea. Glass frogs in the rainforests of Central and South America have see-through skin on their bellies. But blood is red, and red is easy to spot. In 2022, scientists found that a sleeping glass frog hides almost all its red blood cells inside its liver. That makes it about two or three times more see-through. When it wakes, the blood flows out again. Nobody yet knows how the frog stops this packed blood from clotting.
examples: A jellyfish can be very hard to see in clear water.
A glass frog's heart can sometimes be seen beating through its skin.
Some tiny shrimps and baby fish are almost transparent.
explanations.art: A glass frog asleep on a leaf, its body pale and see-through, with a small shiny liver visible inside.
explanations.context: This card is about animals that are almost see-through, and how it helps them.

explanations.concept: Light that takes thousands of years to leave the Sun
explanations.description: The inside of the Sun is not transparent. It is so packed with hot particles that light cannot travel straight. A bit of light made in the Sun's middle bumps into a particle, bounces off somewhere new, bumps again, and again, millions and millions of times. So it takes a very long time to wander out to the surface. Once it is out, it reaches Earth in about eight minutes. Scientists agree on the wandering. They give different answers for how long it takes, because it is hard to work out.
examples: Some of the sunlight on your face today may have started its journey in the Sun before people built the first cities.
A crowded railway platform is like the Sun's inside: you cannot walk straight across, you keep bumping and turning.

perspectives.explanation: About 10,000 years or a little more.
As long as 170,000 years. NASA gives the whole range, from about 10,000 to 170,000 years, because the answer depends on how the Sun's insides are modelled.

explanations.art: A cut-away Sun with a tiny light dot zigzagging through a crowd of particles from the centre to the edge.
explanations.context: This card is about how the inside of the Sun is not see-through, and how long light takes to escape it.

explanations.concept: The universe was once a glowing fog
explanations.definition: For about the first 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe was opaque. Then it cooled and became transparent, and the light from that moment still reaches us today.
explanations.description: Long ago the whole universe was hot, crowded and full of loose tiny particles. Light kept bumping into them, like light in thick fog. Nothing could be seen across it. As the universe stretched and cooled, the particles joined into atoms. Suddenly light could travel freely. The universe became transparent. That very old light is still all around us. It has stretched into a kind of invisible light called the cosmic microwave background. Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found it by accident in 1965. A little of the snow on an old TV screen came from it.
examples: Morning fog in winter over a field: you cannot see the trees until it clears.
Satellites called COBE, WMAP and Planck have made maps of this oldest light.
explanations.art: A timeline from left to right: a bright foggy glow, then a clearing where light rays shoot freely across to a tiny modern Earth.
explanations.context: This card follows the idea of opaque and transparent all the way out to the whole universe.

explanations.concept: Matter that is perfectly see-through: dark matter
explanations.description: Stars and galaxies move as if they are being pulled by much more stuff than we can see. Vera Rubin, an American astronomer, measured this carefully in the 1970s by watching how fast stars go round in galaxies. Scientists call the missing stuff dark matter. It does not give out light, and it does not block light. Light goes straight through it. So it is more see-through than the cleanest glass. Nobody knows what it is.
examples: Light from far galaxies is bent by the pull of dark matter, but never blocked by it.
There seems to be about five times more dark matter than ordinary matter.

perspectives.explanation: Dark matter is made of a kind of tiny particle we have not found yet. Big experiments deep underground are searching for it.

perspectives.who: Some scientists, like Mordehai Milgrom, who proposed this in 1983
perspectives.explanation: There may be no dark matter. Maybe gravity works a little differently over huge distances than we think.

explanations.art: A spiral galaxy inside a faint, see-through cloud drawn with dotted lines, with light rays passing straight through it.
explanations.context: This card goes out into space, to stuff that light passes straight through.

explanations.concept: Nothing is perfectly transparent, and light has a little luck
explanations.description: Even the clearest glass is not perfect. At night, in a lit room, you can see a faint picture of the room in the window. That is because a little light bounces back at each surface of the glass, about 4 parts in every 100. Physicists found that light comes in tiny packets. Nobody can say in advance which packet will go through and which will bounce back. Only the share is fixed. Some scientists think this chance is truly part of nature. Others wonder if something hidden decides. Here 'deciding' does not mean anyone's mind. It is still argued about.
examples: Fibres of very pure glass carry internet light under the oceans for many kilometres.
Katharine Burr Blodgett, an American scientist, invented a thin coating in 1938 that made glass even clearer, by stopping most of that bounce.

perspectives.explanation: Which packet of light goes through is truly a matter of chance. Only the share can be predicted.
There may be hidden details we cannot yet measure, which decide each packet's path.

explanations.art: A window at night faintly showing the lit room, with a few tiny light dots bouncing back and most passing through.
explanations.context: This card is about how even clear glass is not perfectly see-through, and the chance involved.

agreed.text: Materials can be sorted by how much light they let through: transparent, translucent and opaque.
agreed.evidence: Shine a torch through glass, butter paper and steel, and anyone can see the difference on the wall. Children all over the world do this test in class.

agreed.text: Translucent and white materials scatter light at many tiny edges inside them.
agreed.evidence: Fill the gaps with oil or water and many of them turn clearer. Grind clear glass into powder and it turns white.

agreed.text: Whether a material is see-through depends on its thickness and on the kind of light.
agreed.evidence: Thin gold leaf lets light through, but a gold coin does not. Glass passes the light we see but stops much ultraviolet light, which scientists measure with special meters.

agreed.text: Ordinary glass is a solid. It does not slowly flow.
agreed.evidence: Edgar Zanotto, a Brazilian scientist, worked out in 1998 that cathedral glass would take far longer than the age of the universe to sag noticeably. Old Roman glass has kept its shape for 2,000 years.

agreed.text: The universe became transparent about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
agreed.evidence: The light from that moment, the cosmic microwave background, was found in 1965 and has been mapped very carefully by satellites.

challenging.who: A common idea, especially in children's stories about invisible things
challenging.for: You look straight through a clean window and often do not notice the glass.
challenging.against: You can still see a glass of water. A little light bounces off its surfaces, and its edges bend light. That is why birds sometimes fly into windows, but people rarely walk into a glass of water. Truly invisible things would have to bounce and bend no light at all.
challenging.context: This card looks at the idea that see-through means invisible.

challenging.claim: Glass is a liquid that flows very slowly. That is why old church windows are thicker at the bottom.
challenging.who: A popular story told for over 100 years, even by some teachers
challenging.for: Some very old windows in Europe really are thicker at the bottom.
challenging.against: Old glass was made by spinning a blob into a disc, so it came out uneven. Builders usually put the thick edge at the bottom, but not always. Some old panes have their thick edge at the top. Measurements show glass would take far longer than the age of the universe to sag at room temperature.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous myth: that old glass flows like very slow honey.

challenging.claim: Darker sunglasses always protect your eyes better.
challenging.who: A common belief when buying sunglasses
challenging.for: Dark lenses cut down a lot of the light we can see, so they feel more protective.
challenging.against: Darkness and ultraviolet protection are different things. A dark lens with no ultraviolet filter lets the harmful light through. Eye doctors say to look for a 'UV400' or '100% UV protection' label. A light lens with that label protects better than a dark one without it.
challenging.context: This card is about choosing sunglasses, and whether darker means safer.

challenging.claim: Nothing is truly opaque. Make anything thin enough and some light gets through.
challenging.for: Gold leaf, a thin leaf, your fingertips and even a thin slice of rock let some light through. Geologists study rocks by slicing them so thin that light shines through.
challenging.against: Some materials, like thick metal, stop practically all light. In daily life, calling them opaque is simply true.
challenging.context: This card asks whether anything is completely opaque.

challenging.claim: Light that goes into a translucent material is lost.
challenging.who: A natural guess, because the picture disappears
challenging.for: Behind butter paper, the clear picture is gone.
challenging.against: Most of the light is still there. It has only been mixed up in direction. A room behind a frosted window is still bright. Only the picture, the neat order of the light, is lost.
challenging.context: This card is about what happens to light inside translucent things.

challenging.who: A common assumption, since glass is so ordinary
challenging.for: People have made glass for over 4,000 years. We know exactly how to make every kind of glass we use.
challenging.against: Scientists still argue about what glass really is. Its atoms are jumbled like a liquid's, yet it is stiff like a solid. In 1995 the Nobel Prize winner Philip Anderson called the nature of glass perhaps the deepest unsolved problem in the science of solids.
challenging.context: This card is about a surprise: scientists still argue about what glass really is.

big_questions.q: Your hand lets red light through. So is your hand opaque or translucent? Who decides?
big_questions.hint: Think about how thick the material is, and what kind of light we are talking about.

big_questions.q: Sugar is white, but sugar water is clear. Where did the sugar go?
big_questions.hint: Taste the water. Is the sugar gone, or just too small to bounce light?

big_questions.q: Why does oil make paper see-through?
big_questions.hint: What is in the tiny gaps between the paper threads before, and after?

big_questions.q: If a material let every kind of light through and bounced none back, could you see it at all?
big_questions.hint: How do you see a clean glass of water on the table?

big_questions.q: A thin curtain hides you by day but not at night. Is privacy something a material has, or something the light makes?
big_questions.hint: Remember the story of the chikan curtain, where the bright side showed up.

big_questions.q: When is it good to let people see through, and when is it good to hide? Think of homes, schools and governments.
big_questions.hint: Some people say a fair government should be 'transparent'. What do you think they mean?

big_questions.q: Some sparkly powders in paint and makeup are made from a mineral called mica, dug in Jharkhand. Who digs it, and should we ask?
big_questions.hint: Behind a shiny thing there are often hands we never see. Is it fair not to know?

big_questions.q: The universe was once a fog that light could not cross. What is still hidden from us today, like a fog?
big_questions.hint: Think of dark matter, which no light shows us.

big_questions.q: A glass frog hides its blood to become see-through. If you could be see-through for a day, would you want to be?
big_questions.hint: Would you feel safer, or more alone?

big_questions.q: Ammi's stitched flowers could only be seen properly with light behind them, from outside. Is there work in your home that is hard to see?
big_questions.hint: Who does a quiet job that you only notice when it is not done?

story.title: The Flowers That Bloomed at Night
story.note: Lucknow's chikan embroidery on fine cotton muslin is real, and so is the way a thin curtain hides the dim side and shows the bright side. Meenu, her family and the lane are made up.
text: Meenu lived above her father's cloth shop, in the old part of Lucknow. The lane outside was so narrow that two rickshaws could not pass. Her window looked down on it. Across the window hung a curtain her mother had made. It was white muslin, as thin as a breath, and Ammi had stitched it all over with white flowers. That kind of stitching is called chikan. It had taken her four months, sewing in the quiet hour after everyone else had gone to sleep.

In the daytime, Meenu loved that curtain. She could sit behind it and watch the whole lane. The man frying jalebis in a black pan. The goat that ate posters. The postman who sang old film songs. And nobody ever looked up at her. Once she waved at Mr. Rizvi from the sweet shop. He looked straight at her window and did not wave back. He saw nothing at all.
"It's a magic curtain," Meenu told her little brother Faiz. "I can see out, and nobody can see in."

Five days before Diwali, Meenu began her secret. Abba's old paper lantern, the kandil that hung over the shop door every year, had torn in last year's rain. "Never mind," he had said. "The shop can be dark this year." Meenu decided it would not be dark. She would make him a new one. She had red kite paper, thin sticks of bamboo, a pot of glue made of flour and water, and eleven rupees of her own, spent on gold paper for the edges.

After school there was homework, and then tuition. So she worked at night. She shut her door, lit the lamp on her desk, and cut and glued until her eyes stung. The curtain hung quietly beside her. The lane beyond it was dark.
On the third morning, Abba put down his tea and looked at her over his glasses. "Meenu-beti," he said, "who was the giant in your window last night? She had scissors as big as a door."
Faiz laughed so hard that milk came out of his nose. "I saw her too, from the lane," he said. "She was cutting out a big square. Then she put her finger in her mouth, because she cut it."
Meenu's face went hot. Abba only smiled and went down to open the shop. He did not ask what she was making. But Meenu sat very still. How had they seen? The curtain was magic. She had tested it.

That afternoon she tested it again. She went down into the lane, stood by the jalebi pan and looked up at her own window. She saw a square of white cloth, glowing a little in the sun. Nothing behind it. No desk, no bed, not even the dark shape of the cupboard. The magic was working.
That evening she tried it the other way round. She put Faiz in her room with the lamp lit, and told him to dance. Then she ran down the stairs, out into the lane, and looked up.

There was Faiz. Not his face, but all of him, a dark dancing shape, as clear as a puppet at a puppet show. She could see his elbows. She could see the lamp flame, bright as a seed, and the cupboard behind him. And across the whole curtain, Ammi's white flowers had turned dark. They stood out like a painted garden, every petal and every leaf, black against the glowing cloth.
Meenu stood in the lane for a long time. Ammi came out to buy coriander and found her there. "What are you staring at?"
"Your flowers," said Meenu. "They're dark. In the day they're white."

Ammi looked up. She had never seen her curtain from the lane at night. She tilted her head. "Where the cloth is thin, the light gets through," she said slowly. "Where I stitched, the thread is thick. The light can't get through the thick parts so easily."

"And the curtain isn't magic," said Meenu. She worked it out aloud. "In the day, the lane is bright and my room is dim. At night, my room is bright and the lane is dark. Whoever is on the bright side shows. The curtain only hides the dim side."

For the last two nights, Meenu took the heavy old razai out of the trunk. It was a thick cotton quilt that no light could get through. She hung it over the window, in front of the muslin. From the lane, Faiz reported, her window was now just a dark square, like every other window. She finished the lantern on the last night. When she held Abba's torch inside it, the red paper glowed all over. You could not see the torch at all, only a warm red light.

On Diwali evening, when the lane was full of lamps and noise, Meenu took the razai down. She hung the new kandil just inside her window, behind the muslin, with a small electric bulb inside it, the way Abba always hung his. She switched off her desk lamp. Then she ran down to the shop and pulled Abba out by the hand into the lane.
"Look up," she said.

Abba looked up. The window glowed red, like a coal. In the middle hung the dark shape of a lantern with its gold edges. And all around it, dark against the red light, bloomed Ammi's flowers. There were hundreds of them, every one she had stitched in all those quiet hours. People in the lane stopped and looked up too. The jalebi man said, "Wah." Ammi came out of the shop with a needle still in her hand. She stood beside them and said nothing at all for a long while.

Later, Abba carried the kandil down and hung it over the shop door, where it belonged. But every evening of that Diwali, Meenu switched on a bulb behind the curtain, so that the lane could see the garden that had been there all along.
story.epiphany: For the parent: thin muslin is translucent. Through it, you can see from the dim side into the bright side, but not the other way. By day the lane is bright, so Meenu sees out and is hidden. At night her lamp makes her room the bright side, so the lane sees her. The thick stitches block more light than the thin cloth. So they look white when light falls on them from the front, and dark when light comes from behind. The quilt is opaque and hides everything. Meenu solves her problem by understanding the light, not by finding a better curtain. The story also quietly asks whose patient work goes unseen until someone looks from the right side.
ask: In the daytime, why could Meenu see the lane, but Mr. Rizvi could not see her?
Why could Faiz see Meenu's shadow at night, through the same curtain?
Why did Ammi's white flowers look dark from the lane at night?
Why did hanging the razai over the window keep Meenu's secret?
Ammi had never seen her own flowers from the lane at night. Why do you think she was quiet for so long?

flow.say: Every card is a job. For each job, we choose a material. Should it be clear, so we see straight through? Cloudy, so light comes in but no picture? Or blocked, so no light gets through?
flow.kid: Put out the three mats. Mix up the cards. For each job, pick clear, cloudy or blocked.
flow.context: This is the first step of Clear, Cloudy or Blocked?, a card game about choosing materials for jobs. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the card 'A bathroom window'. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise with one card. 'A bathroom window.' Which mat does it go on?
flow.kid: Practice card: a bathroom window. Clear, cloudy or blocked? Tap your answer.

good: We want light, but we want privacy too.

check.q: A bathroom window. What does it need?
check.why: A bathroom needs daylight, but nobody should see in. Translucent glass, like frosted glass, does both. Picking clear forgets about privacy. Picking blocked forgets that a window's job is to let light in.

flow.context: This is a practice round of the game Clear, Cloudy or Blocked?. You choose the right kind of material for a bathroom window.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player draws a card, reads it out and puts it on a mat. 2. They say why. 3. They name one real material that would work. 4. Give a lamp token for each good reason.
flow.say: When you put your card down, tell me why, and tell me one real material that would do the job.
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card. Put it on a mat. Say why. Name a material. A good reason wins a 🪔 token.
flow.parent: Some cards are tricky on purpose. A greenhouse needs transparent or translucent cover, because plants need light. A kite that glows needs translucent paper. A medicine bottle and a milk packet need opaque or dark material, because light spoils them. A tracing sheet needs to be translucent but thin enough to see the picture when it touches it. Accept any choice with a good reason.
flow.context: This is the main part of the game Clear, Cloudy or Blocked?. Players choose materials for everyday jobs and explain why.

flow.do: When a TRY IT card comes up, stop and do it together. Everyone guesses first.
flow.say: Before we try it, everyone guess what will happen. Then we'll see who was right.
flow.kid: A TRY IT card! Guess first. Then try it. Were you right?

ask.q: Why did the oil spot on the paper go see-through?
good: The oil filled the little gaps in the paper.
Light did not bounce about so much.

flow.think: Your hand lets a little red light through. So which mat does a hand belong on?
flow.context: This step of the game Clear, Cloudy or Blocked? is for the TRY IT cards, where everyone does a quick test with light.

flow.do: 1. Count everyone's tokens to find the winner. 2. Look at the three piles together.

flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who won? Which card was hardest to place? Why?

games.title: Guess Behind the Sheet
games.players: 2 or more players, with a grown-up to work the torch
games.context: This is a guessing game. A torch shines on things from behind a white bedsheet. Players guess each thing from the shadow it makes. Opaque things make dark shadows, translucent things make pale ones, and transparent things make almost none.

a hand making a bird shape

printables.title: Shadow score sheet
items: Dark, pale or almost no shadow?

rules: Hang a white bedsheet across a doorway, or hold it up between two chairs.
The hider stands behind the sheet with the torch and the objects. The guessers sit in front, in the dark.
The hider holds one object between the torch and the sheet.
Guessers say what it is, and whether its shadow is dark, pale or almost none.
One point for the right object. One more for the right group: opaque, translucent or transparent.

setup.art: A white bedsheet pinned across a doorway in a dark room, with a torch shining onto it from behind.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a white sheet across a doorway. Make the room dark.

setup.art: Behind the sheet, a child holding a glass of water between a torch and the sheet.
setup.caption: 2. The hider holds one object between the torch and the sheet.
