flow.do: 1. Hang a white bedsheet across a doorway, or between two chairs. 2. Switch off the lights. 3. Stand behind the sheet with the torch, about 2 metres back. 4. Put the objects on a stool beside you.
flow.say: I'll hold something behind the sheet, with the torch behind it. You'll only see its shadow. Guess what it is. Then tell me if its shadow is dark, pale or hardly there.
flow.kid: Sit in front of the sheet. A grown-up will hold things behind it. Guess each thing from its shadow.
flow.parent: Keep the torch steady and well back, so the shadows are sharp. Never let a child stand on chairs to hang the sheet.
flow.context: This is the first step of Guess Behind the Sheet, a shadow-guessing game with a bedsheet and a torch. Here you set it up.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the objects one at a time, in any order. 2. Let the guessers shout their guesses. 3. Show each object after the guess. 4. Mark the score sheet.
flow.say: What is it? And is its shadow dark, pale or almost none?
flow.kid: What is it? Is the shadow dark, pale or hardly there? Say both.

ask.q: Why does the glass of water make a pale shadow with a bright spot?
good: The glass is clear, so most light gets through, but its edges bend some light.

check.q: The steel spoon made a very dark shadow. So the spoon is…
check.why: A dark shadow means almost no light got through. So the spoon is opaque. Picking translucent usually means mixing up 'shiny' with 'lets light through'. A shiny spoon sends light back, but none goes through it.

flow.context: This is the main part of Guess Behind the Sheet. You guess each object from its shadow.

flow.do: Swap. Let a child be the hider while the grown-up holds the torch.
flow.say: Now you choose something to hide. Can you find something that makes a pale shadow? Can you trick us?
flow.kid: Your turn to hide things. Can you find something with a pale shadow?
flow.think: A leaf made a pale shadow, and you could see its veins. Why do the veins look darker?
flow.context: This is the last step of Guess Behind the Sheet. Children take turns to choose the objects.

experiments.title: The Gap Test: how far until the words blur?
experiments.question: How see-through is each material? How far can we lift it off a page before we can no longer read the words?
experiments.predict: Before you test, line up the materials. Put the one you think you can lift highest first, and the one that blurs words soonest last.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, change only the material. Use the same card of letters, in the same light, and keep your eyes at the same height every time. Test each material 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: Try 1: gap when the words blurred (cm)

materials.item: a card with the word LIGHT written on it in big letters, about 2 cm tall
pieces of 5 materials, each about as big as a postcard: cling film, a thin plastic carry bag, butter paper, a cotton handkerchief, a paper tissue
a ruler
a stack of books about 30 cm high, to rest your chin on
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: This test is safe. Do it in daylight by a window, or under a bright room light. Never use the Sun directly.

schedule.what: Guess the order. Test each material 3 times. Write down the gaps. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart, with one bar for each material. Make each bar as tall as its middle gap.
experiments.context: This is the gap test. You lay a material flat on a card of big letters, then slowly lift it. You measure how high you can lift it before the words blur. The higher you can lift it, the more see-through it is.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how high each material could be lifted before the words blurred
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different. Cling film never blurred, so we wrote the ruler's top, 30 cm.

setup.art: A card with the word LIGHT in big letters on a table, with a square of butter paper lying flat on top of it so the letters show through.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the material flat on the card of letters.

setup.art: A child resting their chin on a stack of books, lifting the butter paper slowly above the card with a ruler standing upright beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Keep your chin on the books. Lift the material slowly.

setup.art: A close-up of the ruler beside the raised butter paper, the letters below now blurry, a finger pointing at the 2 cm mark.
setup.caption: 3. When the word blurs, stop. Read the gap on the ruler.

flow.do: 1. Write LIGHT on a card in big letters, about 2 cm tall. 2. Cut postcard-sized pieces of the 5 materials. 3. Ask your child to put the materials in a line, from most see-through to least.
flow.say: Here are five materials. Which one do you think you can see through best? Put them in a line. Put the most see-through first.
flow.kid: Look at the five materials. Which can you see through best? Put them in a line. Best first.

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?
good: I can see my hand through it.

flow.context: This is the first step of the gap test. You will find out how see-through each material is, by lifting it off a page of words.

flow.do: 1. Put the card on the table near a window or under a bright light. 2. Stand the ruler upright beside it, with 0 at the table. 3. Make a stack of books next to the card. 4. Your child rests their chin on the books, so their eyes stay at the same height.
flow.say: We'll keep your eyes at the same height every time, so the test is fair. Rest your chin on the books.
flow.kid: Put your chin on the books. Keep it there the whole time. That keeps the test fair.
flow.parent: The chin rest matters. If the eyes move closer or further, the results change. Keep the room light the same for every try.
flow.context: This step sets up the gap test fairly: the same card, the same light and the eyes at the same height.

flow.do: 1. Lay the first material flat on the card. 2. Ask: can you read the word? 3. Lift it slowly, about 1 cm each second, keeping it flat. 4. Your child says 'Stop!' the moment the word blurs so it cannot be read. 5. Read the gap on the ruler and write it down. 6. Do this 3 times for each material.
flow.say: Can you read the word now? Good. I'll lift it slowly. Shout 'stop' the moment you can't read it any more.
flow.kid: Can you read the word? Now watch it as the material lifts. Shout 'Stop!' when you can't read it.
flow.parent: Butter paper and tissue usually let you read the word when they touch the card, then blur within 1 or 2 cm. That surprises most children. If a material never blurs, like cling film, write the top of the ruler. To find the middle value, put the three numbers in order and take the middle one.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.context: This is the main step of the gap test. You lift each material off the card until the word blurs, and measure the gap.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the middle values, with one bar for each material.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. Each material gets a bar. The taller the bar, the higher we could lift it before the word blurred.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each material. Make it as tall as its middle number. Taller means more see-through.

check.q: In the gap test, the plastic bag could be lifted 6 cm and the tissue only 1 cm. Which is more see-through?
check.why: The plastic bag could be lifted further before the word blurred, so it jumbles light less. It is more see-through. Picking the tissue usually means thinking that a bigger number means more blur. Here the number is how far the picture survived.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how high each material could be lifted before the words blurred
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like.

flow.context: This step of the gap test turns your measurements into a bar chart.

flow.do: Sort the five materials into transparent, translucent and opaque, using the results.
flow.say: Which material never blurred? That one is transparent. Which ones let light through but lost the word? Those are translucent.
flow.kid: Which one never blurred? That's transparent. Which let light through but lost the word? Those are translucent.
flow.think: Butter paper let you read the word when it touched the card. So is it transparent when it touches, and translucent when it is lifted?
flow.context: This step of the gap test uses your results to sort the materials into transparent and translucent.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: cling film is the most see-through. What I saw: the word never blurred with cling film, but with tissue it blurred at 1 cm. Why: the tissue has lots of tiny threads that bounce the light about, and cling film is smooth all through.
flow.context: This is the last step of the gap test. You say what you found, the evidence, and why.

experiments.title: The Oil Spot Window
experiments.question: Can a drop of oil or water make paper more see-through? Does it last?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will a drop of water make paper more see-through, less see-through, or the same? What about a drop of oil? Which will last longer?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same sheet of paper for all three spots, so the paper is the same. Use one drop of each, the same size. Score all the spots in the same light.

materials.item: a sheet of plain white paper, like printer paper
cooking oil, like coconut or sunflower oil
a spoon of water
a dropper or a cotton bud
a newspaper or a printed page to read through the paper
a pencil

experiments.safety: Use a little oil only, and wipe up any spills so nobody slips. Wash your hands after.

schedule.what: Make a dry spot, a water spot and an oil spot. Score them. Wait one hour and score them again.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with a score for each spot. 0 means no light comes through. 1 means a glow. 2 means you see shapes. 3 means you can read words through it.
experiments.context: In this experiment you put a drop of water and a drop of oil on plain paper. Then you see whether each spot turns more see-through, and whether it stays that way.

setup.art: A sheet of white paper with three pencil circles labelled DRY, WATER and OIL.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three circles on the paper: dry, water and oil.

setup.art: A child putting one drop of oil in one circle with a cotton bud, and a drop of water in another.
setup.caption: 2. Put one drop of water in one circle and one drop of oil in another.

setup.art: The paper held over a newspaper: the words show clearly through the oil spot, less through the water spot, and hardly at all through the dry circle.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the paper over printed words. Score each spot.

flow.do: 1. Draw three circles on the paper, each as big as a coin. 2. Label them DRY, WATER and OIL. 3. Ask your child to guess what each drop will do.
flow.say: Paper is made of tiny threads with air between them. What do you think a drop of water will do to it? And a drop of oil?
flow.kid: Draw three circles. Write DRY, WATER and OIL. Guess what each drop will do.
flow.context: This is the first step of the oil spot experiment. You guess what a drop of oil and a drop of water will do to plain paper.

flow.do: 1. Put one drop of water in the WATER circle. 2. Put one drop of oil in the OIL circle. 3. Rub each gently with a clean fingertip so it spreads to fill the circle.
flow.say: One drop each. Rub it in gently, so it fills the circle.
flow.kid: Put one drop of water in its circle. One drop of oil in its circle. Rub gently.
flow.context: This step of the oil spot experiment puts the drops on the paper.

flow.do: 1. Lay the paper over a newspaper page. 2. Score each circle from 0 to 3. 3. Then hold the paper up to a window and look at the light through each circle.
flow.say: Look through each circle at the words. Score it. Zero is no light. One is a glow. Two is shapes. Three is words you can read.
flow.kid: Put the paper on a newspaper. Score each circle from 0 to 3. Three means you can read the words.

check.q: Which spot let you see the newspaper words best?
check.why: The oil filled the air gaps between the paper threads. Light passes from thread to oil without bouncing much, so the words came through. Water works a little too, but less. Picking the dry spot usually means thinking that adding anything to paper must block more light.

flow.context: This step of the oil spot experiment scores how see-through each spot is, from 0 to 3.

flow.do: Leave the paper flat in a safe place for one hour.
flow.say: Now we wait one hour. What do you think will happen to each spot?
flow.kid: Leave the paper for one hour. Guess what will change.
flow.context: In this step of the oil spot experiment, you leave the paper for an hour to see if the spots change.

flow.do: 1. Lay the paper over the newspaper again. 2. Score each circle again. 3. Compare with the first scores.
flow.say: Look again. Which spot changed? Why do you think the water spot went back to white?
flow.kid: Score each circle again. Which one changed? Why?

ask.q: Why did the water spot go back to white?
good: Air came back into the gaps.

flow.parent: The water spot usually goes back to white as it dries, because air fills the gaps again. The oil spot stays see-through, because oil does not dry away. Long ago, before glass was cheap, many people used oiled or greased paper in their windows. Butter paper is made in a way that leaves very few air gaps, which is why it is translucent.
flow.context: This step of the oil spot experiment checks the spots again after an hour.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: oil makes paper more see-through, and it lasts. What I saw: the oil spot scored 3 and stayed 3. The water spot scored 2, then went back to 1. Why: oil and water fill the air gaps so light bounces less. Water dries away, oil does not.
flow.context: This is the last step of the oil spot experiment. You say what you found, the evidence and why.

experiments.title: Sunglasses Lab: when do they help?
experiments.question: Do sunglasses help us see better in bright light? Do they help indoors?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will you read smaller letters with sunglasses on, or without, in bright light outside? What about inside a dim room?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same letter chart, stand the same 3 big steps away, and change only the sunglasses and the place.
results_table: Smallest row I can read without sunglasses
Smallest row I can read with sunglasses

materials.item: a pair of sunglasses, best with a UV400 label
a letter chart: six rows of letters on white paper, getting smaller, numbered 1 to 6
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Never look at the Sun, with or without sunglasses. Sunglasses do not make it safe. A grown-up goes outside with you.

schedule.what: Make a letter chart. Read it outside in bright light, then inside in a dim room, with and without sunglasses.

experiments.record: Write the number of the smallest row you could read, each time.
experiments.context: In this experiment you read a chart of letters that get smaller and smaller. You read it with and without sunglasses, outside in bright light and inside in a dim room.

setup.art: A sheet of white paper with six rows of letters getting smaller, row 1 big and row 6 tiny, numbered down the side.
setup.caption: 1. Make a chart with six rows of letters, big to small.

setup.art: A grown-up holding the chart in a bright courtyard while a child stands three steps away in sunglasses, with their back to the Sun.
setup.caption: 2. Outside, stand 3 steps away. Read it with and without sunglasses.

setup.art: The same child in a dim room with curtains drawn, squinting at the chart with sunglasses on.
setup.caption: 3. Then do the same inside, in a dim room.

flow.do: 1. On white paper, write six rows of letters. 2. Make row 1 about 4 cm tall, then 3, 2, 1.5, 1 and half a centimetre. 3. Number the rows 1 to 6.
flow.say: We'll make an eye chart. Each row has smaller letters. We'll see which is the smallest row you can read.
flow.kid: Write six rows of letters. Make each row smaller. Number them 1 to 6.
flow.context: This is the first step of the sunglasses lab. You make a chart of letters to test how well you can see.

flow.do: 1. Go outside to a bright place in the late morning. 2. Hold the chart where the sunlight falls on it. 3. Your child stands 3 big steps away, with their back to the Sun. 4. They read the smallest row they can, without sunglasses, then with.
flow.say: Keep your back to the Sun. Never look at it. Read me the smallest row you can. Now put on the sunglasses and try again.
flow.kid: Turn your back to the Sun. Never look at it. Read the smallest row. Now try with sunglasses.
flow.parent: White paper in sunshine causes glare. Many children read one row smaller with sunglasses, but some see no difference. Both are honest results.
flow.context: This step of the sunglasses lab tests reading the chart outside in bright light.

flow.do: 1. Go into a dim room, with the curtains closed and one small light on. 2. Hold the chart 3 big steps away. 3. Your child reads it without sunglasses, then with.
flow.say: Now we're inside, where it's dim. Read the smallest row. Now with the sunglasses.
flow.kid: Now read the chart in a dim room. Then with sunglasses. Is it harder?

check.q: In the dim room, the sunglasses made the letters…
check.why: Sunglasses are tinted. They let only part of the light through. In bright sun that cuts glare. In a dim room there is little light to start with, so cutting it makes reading harder. Picking 'easier' usually means thinking that sunglasses always help you see.

flow.context: This step of the sunglasses lab tests reading the chart in a dim room.

flow.do: Look at the label on the sunglasses together. Look for 'UV400' or '100% UV protection'.
flow.say: The darkness of the lenses is one thing. Blocking ultraviolet light, which we can't see, is another. The label tells us which.
flow.kid: Find the label on the sunglasses. Does it say UV400? That means they block ultraviolet light.
flow.parent: Dark lenses without ultraviolet protection can be worse than none, because the eyes let in more light behind dark lenses. Cheap toy sunglasses often have no ultraviolet filter.
flow.context: In this step of the sunglasses lab you check whether the sunglasses block ultraviolet light, the invisible light that can harm eyes.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: When do sunglasses help? When do they get in the way? What did you see, and why?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: sunglasses help in bright sun, but not indoors. What I saw: outside I read row 5 with sunglasses and row 4 without. Inside I read row 4 without and only row 2 with them. Why: they let only part of the light through. That cuts glare in sun, but leaves too little light indoors.
flow.context: This is the last step of the sunglasses lab. You say what you found, the evidence and why.

activities.title: Glowing Hands and the See-Through Hunt

materials.item: a torch
three bowls or trays labelled CLEAR, CLOUDY and BLOCKED

activities.safety: Never shine a torch into anyone's eyes. Only touch things you are allowed to carry.

schedule.what: Make your fingers glow with a torch. Then hunt the house for clear, cloudy and blocked things.

activities.record: Draw your glowing hand. Then list four things you found for each group.
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You make your fingers glow red with a torch, then hunt the house for things that let light through, blur it or block it.

setup.art: A child in a dark room holding a torch under their fingertips, which glow red.
setup.caption: 1. In a dark room, press a torch under your fingertips.

setup.art: Three trays labelled CLEAR, CLOUDY and BLOCKED on a floor, holding a glass, a sheet of butter paper and a steel plate.
setup.caption: 2. Set out three trays: clear, cloudy and blocked.

setup.art: A child holding a plastic bottle up to a window to see if light comes through.
setup.caption: 3. Hold each thing up to the light. Put it on a tray.

flow.do: 1. Make a room as dark as you can. 2. Your child presses the torch glass against the tips of their fingers and switches it on. 3. Ask what they notice.
flow.say: Look at your fingers. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Make the room dark. Press the torch under your fingertips. Switch it on. What do you see?

good: I can see darker lines inside.

flow.parent: The red glow is light passing through skin and blood. Red light gets through best. Don't explain much yet. Let the child wonder.
flow.context: This is the first step of the glowing hands activity. You find out that some light can pass through your own hand.

flow.do: 1. Put out the three labelled trays. 2. Your child collects things from around the house. 3. They hold each one up to a window or the torch. 4. They put it on the CLEAR, CLOUDY or BLOCKED tray.
flow.say: Find things around the house. Hold each one up to the light. Can you see clearly through it? Then it's clear. Does light get through, but no picture? Cloudy. No light at all? Blocked.
flow.kid: Find things around the house. Hold each to the light. Clear, cloudy or blocked? Put it on a tray.

check.q: You hold a plastic carry bag up to the window. Light comes through, but the tree outside looks blurry. Which tray?
check.why: Light gets through, but the picture is blurry. That is translucent, the cloudy tray. Picking CLEAR usually means noticing the light but not checking the picture. Picking BLOCKED forgets that some light did come through.

flow.context: This step of the hunt activity sorts things from around the house into clear, cloudy and blocked.

flow.do: Look at the three trays together.
flow.say: Was anything hard to put on a tray? Where would your hand go?
flow.kid: Look at your trays. Which thing was hardest to sort? Where does your hand go?
flow.think: Is your hand cloudy or blocked? Does it depend on the light?
flow.context: This is the last step of the hunt. You look back at the trays and the tricky things.

activities.title: Where Did the Sugar Go?

materials.item: a clear glass of warm water
two spoons of sugar
a spoon for stirring
a small dark plate

activities.safety: Use warm water from the tap, not boiling water.

schedule.what: Look at a pile of sugar. Stir it into water. Watch the white vanish.

activities.record: Draw the sugar before, during and after stirring. Draw the tiny pieces you can't see, too.
activities.context: In this activity you stir white sugar into water and watch it vanish. It shows why piles of tiny grains look white, but the same stuff dissolved is clear.

setup.art: A small white pile of sugar on a dark plate next to a clear glass of water.
setup.caption: 1. Put a little pile of sugar on a dark plate.

setup.art: A spoon stirring sugar into a glass of water, the water cloudy with swirling grains.
setup.caption: 2. Tip the sugar into the water and stir.

setup.art: The same glass now completely clear, with a zoomed-in circle showing tiny sugar molecules spread among water molecules.
setup.caption: 3. Keep stirring until the water is clear again.

flow.do: 1. Put a little pile of sugar on the dark plate. 2. Look at one grain closely. 3. Then look at the whole pile.
flow.say: Look at one grain of sugar. It's almost clear, like a tiny bit of glass. So why is the pile white?
flow.kid: Look at one sugar grain. It is almost clear. But the pile is white. Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the sugar activity. You look at sugar grains and wonder why a pile of clear grains looks white.

flow.do: 1. Tip the sugar into the warm water. 2. Stir slowly. 3. Watch until the water is clear.
flow.say: Watch the water while you stir. What happens to the white?
flow.kid: Tip the sugar in. Stir slowly. Watch the white disappear.

check.q: Why does a pile of sugar look white, when each grain is almost clear?
options: Sugar is painted white in the factory
Light bounces off the edges of every grain
The grains make their own light
check.why: Each grain has edges. Light bounces off each edge a little. With thousands of grains, the light bounces every way, so the pile looks white. In water, the sugar breaks into molecules too small to bounce light, so the water is clear. Picking 'painted' is a fair guess, but clear sugar crystals called mishri show sugar is not white inside.

flow.context: This step of the sugar activity stirs the sugar into water and asks why the white vanishes.

flow.do: Let your child taste a sip of the water.
flow.say: The sugar is invisible now. Is it gone? Taste and see.
flow.kid: Taste a sip. Is the sugar gone? Or is it still there, just too small to see?
flow.parent: This links to the Roots card, where a teacher in an old Indian book dissolves salt in water to make the same point. The sugar is everywhere in the water, but no light shows it.
flow.think: What else might be all around us, but too small or too clear to see?
flow.context: This is the last step of the sugar activity. You taste the water to check whether the sugar is still there.

activities.title: Cloudy Ice, Clear Ice

materials.item: two small steel bowls or ice trays
tap water
water that a grown-up has boiled and let cool
a freezer
a clean cloth and a rolling pin for crushing ice

activities.safety: Only a grown-up boils the water. Wrap ice in a cloth before crushing it, so no sharp bits fly.

schedule.what: Fill one bowl with tap water and one with boiled, cooled water. Freeze them overnight.
Compare the two ices. Look for bubbles. Crush some ice and see it turn white.

activities.record: Draw both pieces of ice. Mark where the cloudy parts are. Draw the crushed ice too.
activities.context: In this 2-day activity you freeze two bowls of water and see why ice is sometimes clear and sometimes cloudy. Then you crush ice and watch it turn white.

setup.art: Two steel bowls of water side by side, labelled TAP and BOILED, going into a freezer.
setup.caption: 1. Fill one bowl with tap water and one with boiled, cooled water. Freeze overnight.

setup.art: Two blocks of ice on a plate, one with a cloudy white middle full of tiny bubbles, one clearer.
setup.caption: 2. Next day, compare the two blocks of ice.

setup.art: Ice wrapped in a cloth being tapped with a rolling pin, and a heap of white crushed ice beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Crush some ice in a cloth. See it turn white.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up boils some water and lets it cool completely. 2. Fill one bowl with tap water and label it TAP. 3. Fill the other with the cooled boiled water and label it BOILED. 4. Put both in the freezer.
flow.say: Boiling pushes out some of the air hidden in water. Will that change the ice?
flow.kid: Fill one bowl with tap water. A grown-up gives you boiled, cooled water for the other. Freeze both.
flow.wait: Leave them in the freezer overnight
flow.context: This is the first step of the ice activity. You freeze two kinds of water to compare the ice.

flow.do: 1. Take out both ices and put them on a plate. 2. Hold each up to a window. 3. Look for tiny bubbles and cloudy parts.
flow.say: Look through each ice. Where is it clear? Where is it cloudy? What makes the cloudy parts?
flow.kid: Hold each ice up to the window. Where is it clear? Where is it cloudy? Look for bubbles.
flow.parent: The cloudy part is usually in the middle. Water freezes from the outside in, and pushes air into the middle, where it gets trapped as tiny bubbles. Boiled water often makes clearer ice, but it may still be cloudy in the middle. Either result is honest.

check.q: Why is the middle of the ice cloudy?
options: Tiny air bubbles bounce the light about
check.why: Each tiny bubble has an edge where light bounces. Many bubbles make the ice cloudy, just like many sugar grains make sugar white. Picking 'dirty' is a natural guess, but melt the ice and the water is clean.

flow.context: This step of the ice activity compares the two ices and looks for the cloudy parts.

flow.do: 1. Wrap a piece of the clearest ice in a cloth. 2. Tap it with a rolling pin until it is crushed. 3. Open the cloth and look.
flow.say: That ice was nearly clear. Now look at it crushed. What colour is it?
flow.kid: Wrap ice in a cloth. Tap it to crush it. Open it. What colour is it now?
flow.think: Snow is made of clear ice. So why is snow white?
flow.context: This is the last step of the ice activity. You crush clear ice and see it turn white.

activities.title: Day Curtain, Night Curtain

materials.item: a window with a thin curtain, or a thin dupatta hung over a window
a room lamp or torch
a thick bedsheet or quilt

activities.safety: A grown-up goes outside with the child. Stay near the house, and only look into your own home.

schedule.what: In the daytime, look at the window from inside and from outside.
At night, with a lamp on inside, look again from outside. Then try a thick quilt.

activities.record: Draw the window four times: day from inside, day from outside, night from outside, and night with the quilt.
activities.context: In this 2-day activity you test a thin curtain by day and by night. You find out that it hides whoever is on the dim side, and shows whoever is on the bright side.

setup.art: A child inside a room behind a thin curtain in daytime, looking out at a bright street.
setup.caption: 1. In the day, sit behind a thin curtain and look out.

setup.art: A grown-up and child outside in daylight looking up at the same window, which shows only bright white cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Then go outside and look in. What can you see?

setup.art: The same window at night from outside, glowing, with a dark shape of a person moving behind the curtain.
setup.caption: 3. At night, with the lamp on inside, look in again.

flow.do: 1. In the daytime, your child sits inside behind a thin curtain. 2. They look out and say what they can see.
flow.say: What can you see outside through the curtain? Do you think anyone outside can see you?
flow.kid: Sit behind the thin curtain. What can you see outside? Can people see you?
flow.context: This is the first step of the day and night curtain activity. You look out through a thin curtain in the daytime.

flow.do: 1. One person stays inside behind the curtain and waves. 2. The other goes outside and looks at the window. 3. Swap.
flow.say: Can you see me waving? What does the curtain look like from out here?
flow.kid: Go outside with a grown-up. Look at the window. Can you see the person waving?
flow.parent: In the day, the person inside is usually hidden. The curtain looks bright from outside, because daylight bounces off it.
flow.context: This step of the curtain activity checks from outside, in the daytime, whether you can see in.

flow.do: 1. At night, switch on a lamp inside the room. 2. One person moves about behind the curtain. 3. The other goes outside and looks.
flow.say: It's the same curtain. Can you see in now? What changed?
flow.kid: Now it is night. The lamp is on inside. Look from outside. Can you see in?

check.q: At night, with the lamp on inside, people outside can see in. Why?
options: The curtain gets thinner at night
Now the room is the bright side
Curtains only work in the day
check.why: A thin curtain lets a little light through both ways. Whoever is on the bright side shows up to whoever is on the dark side. At night the room is the bright side. Picking 'thinner' usually means thinking the material changed. It is the light that changed.

flow.context: This step of the curtain activity looks at the window from outside at night, with a lamp on inside.

flow.do: 1. Hang a thick quilt or bedsheet over the window. 2. Look from outside again.
flow.say: Now with the thick quilt. Can you see anything?
flow.kid: Hang a thick quilt over the window. Look again. What can you see?
flow.think: Why do many homes have two curtains, one thin and one thick?
flow.context: This is the last step of the curtain activity. You add a thick, opaque quilt and look again.

activities.title: Act It Out: The Light Party

materials.item: an open space, like a room with the furniture pushed back
three paper signs: GLASS, BUTTER PAPER and WALL

activities.safety: Walk, don't run, so nobody bumps heads.

schedule.what: Act out light going through glass, butter paper and a wall.

activities.record: Draw yourself as a bit of light, going through each material.
activities.context: In this drama activity, some people act as bits of light and others act as the atoms of a material. You act out what happens in transparent, translucent and opaque materials.

setup.art: Children standing in neat rows with gaps, as glass atoms, while another child walks straight through the gaps.
setup.caption: 1. GLASS: the atoms stand still in rows. Light walks straight through.

setup.art: Children as paper threads gently turning a walking child this way and that, so they come out facing a new way.
setup.caption: 2. BUTTER PAPER: each atom turns the light a new way.

setup.art: Children linking arms in a tight line as a wall, with a 'light' child stopped and sitting down in front of them.
setup.caption: 3. WALL: the atoms link arms. Light is stopped.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the GLASS sign. 2. Two or three people stand still in a row, with gaps between them. 3. The 'light' walks straight through the gaps from one side of the room to the other.
flow.say: This is glass. The light walks straight through, without turning. Where does it come out?
flow.kid: You are light. Walk straight through the glass atoms. Don't turn. Where do you come out?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Light Party drama. You act out light going straight through glass.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the BUTTER PAPER sign. 2. The atoms stand in a messy cluster. 3. When the 'light' reaches an atom, the atom gently turns it to face a new way. 4. The light keeps walking.
flow.say: This is butter paper. Every thread turns the light a new way. Did the light still get through? Did it come out where it was aiming?
flow.kid: Now the atoms turn you gently, this way and that. Keep walking. Where do you come out?

check.q: In the butter paper game, the light got through but came out in a random place. What does that show?
options: Translucent things let light through but jumble it
check.why: The light got through, so it was not stopped. But it came out facing a new way, so the picture would be lost. That is translucent. Picking 'stop all light' mixes translucent up with opaque.

flow.context: This step of the Light Party drama acts out light being turned about inside butter paper.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the WALL sign. 2. The atoms link arms in a tight line. 3. The light walks up and stops, then sits down, to show the light being soaked up.
flow.say: This is a wall. Light can't get through. Some light bounces back, and some is soaked up and warms the wall.
flow.kid: Now the atoms link arms. You can't get through. Bounce back, or sit down as warmth.
flow.think: If you were a bit of light, which material would you like to visit?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Light Party drama. You act out light being stopped by a wall.

projects.title: The Three-Light Lantern

materials.item: a sheet of thick card or a cereal box
butter paper or tracing paper
a piece of clear plastic from a used food box
glue, tape and child-safe scissors
a battery LED tealight

projects.safety: Use only a battery LED light inside the lantern, never a real flame or diya, because paper burns. A grown-up helps with cutting the windows.

schedule.what: Cut a box shape from card with four windows. Cover one window with clear plastic and two with butter paper. Leave one open with a jaali pattern cut in card.
Let the glue dry. Put the LED light inside in a dark room. Compare the light from each side on the wall.

projects.record: Draw what each side of the lantern shows on the wall. Label it transparent, translucent or opaque with holes.
projects.context: In this 2-day project you build a lantern, like a Diwali kandil, with a different material on each side. Then you light it with an LED and see how each material changes the light on the wall.

setup.art: A flat cut-out card shape for a box with four square windows, on a table with scissors and glue.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a box shape from card, with a window in each side.

setup.art: The box being folded, one window covered with clear plastic, two with butter paper, one with a card jaali pattern of small holes.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the windows: clear plastic, butter paper, and a card jaali.

setup.art: The finished lantern glowing in a dark room: a sharp bright patch, a soft glow and a pattern of spots on the walls.
setup.caption: 3. Light it in the dark. Look at each wall.

flow.do: 1. Draw a cross shape on the card: four squares in a row, each 10 cm, with a square above and below the second one. 2. Cut it out. 3. A grown-up cuts a 6 cm window in each of the four side squares.
flow.say: This will fold into a box. Each side will get a different material, so we can compare them.
flow.kid: Draw the box shape. A grown-up helps cut the windows. Each side gets a different window.
flow.context: This is the first step of the lantern project. You cut out a box with a window on each side.

flow.do: 1. Glue clear plastic over window 1. 2. Glue butter paper over windows 2 and 3. 3. For window 4, glue on card with a pattern of small holes, like a jaali. 4. Fold and tape the box, leaving the top open.
flow.say: One clear window, two cloudy windows, and one blocked window with holes. Which will light the wall most? Which will make the softest light?
flow.kid: Glue clear plastic on one window. Butter paper on two. Card with holes on the last. Fold it into a box.
flow.context: This step of the lantern project covers each window with a different material.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dark. 2. Switch on the LED tealight and put it inside. 3. Put the lantern 30 cm from a wall. 4. Turn it so each side faces the wall in turn.
flow.say: Look at the wall. What does the clear side make? The butter paper side? The jaali side?
flow.kid: Make the room dark. Put the light inside. Turn each side to the wall. What do you see?

check.q: Which side made a soft, even glow with no sharp edges?
check.why: Butter paper scatters light in every direction, so the glow is soft and spread out. That is why lampshades and kandils are often made of translucent paper. The clear side makes a sharp, bright patch. The jaali makes a pattern of spots, because the card blocks light and the holes let it through.

flow.context: This step of the lantern project compares the light from each side in a dark room.

flow.do: Talk about where each kind of light is useful at home.
flow.say: Which side would you want for reading? For a baby's night light? For a party?
flow.kid: Which side is best for reading? For a sleepy baby? For a party?
flow.parent: Good answers: clear for bright reading light, butter paper for a soft night light, the jaali for a pretty pattern. Some children want to make the lantern with all translucent sides next.
flow.context: This is the last step of the lantern project. You decide which kind of light suits which job.

challenges.title: Keep the Light Out, Let Me See In
challenges.problem: Some medicines and milk spoil in light. Design a container that keeps light out, but still lets you check how much is left inside, without opening it.
constraints: Use only things you find at home.
Test it by putting a lit torch inside, in a dark room. No light should leak out when it is closed.
You must be able to tell how full it is, without opening the lid.
materials: black paper, foil, card, cloth and tape
a small torch that fits inside, or a phone torch held at the opening by a grown-up
general: Cover the whole bottle in black paper or foil, so it is opaque.
Make a flap in the cover. Lift the flap to peek at the level, then close it.
Tie a string to a floating cork inside, with the end coming out through the lid, so you can see how high it floats.
creative: Brown and dark-green glass bottles let in less of the light that spoils things. That is why some medicine bottles are brown.
Shake it and listen. Does a full bottle sound different from a half-full one?
Mark the cover with stripes of the same width, and weigh the bottle on a kitchen scale to see how full it is.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own container. Draw it, build it, and do the torch test in the dark. Can a friend tell how full it is without opening it?
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You must make a container that is opaque to keep light out, but still lets you check what is inside.

setup.art: A clear plastic bottle half full of water on a table, beside black paper, foil and tape.
setup.caption: 1. Start with a clear bottle, half full of water.

setup.art: The bottle wrapped in black paper with a small flap cut in the side, lifted to show the water level.
setup.caption: 2. Make it opaque. Find a way to check the level.

setup.art: In a dark room, the wrapped bottle with a torch inside, and a child checking for any light leaking at the seams.
setup.caption: 3. Test it in the dark with a torch inside. Any light leaking?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at a medicine bottle or milk packet at home.
flow.say: Why do you think this medicine bottle is brown, and this milk packet is not see-through?
flow.kid: Look at a medicine bottle or a milk packet. Is it see-through? Why not?
flow.context: This is the first step of the light-proof container challenge. You find out why some containers are not see-through.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a design. 2. They build it from the materials. 3. Fill the bottle halfway with water.
flow.say: Draw your idea first. How will you keep the light out? How will you check how full it is?
flow.kid: Draw your idea. Build it. Keep light out. Find a way to check how full it is.
flow.context: This step of the container challenge is for designing and building.

flow.do: 1. In a dark room, put a lit torch inside the bottle, or hold a phone torch at the opening. 2. Close the cover. 3. Look for any light leaking out.
flow.say: Any light leaking? Where? How could you fix it?
flow.kid: In the dark, put a torch inside. Close it. Can you see any light escaping?

check.q: Light leaks out where two pieces of black paper meet. What is the best fix?
options: Use a clear tape over the gap
Overlap the paper and cover the join with black tape
Leave a small gap so air can get in
check.why: Overlapping the paper and covering the join with black tape makes the whole cover opaque. Clear tape is transparent, so light would pass straight through it. Picking clear tape usually means thinking tape always seals light, but only opaque tape does.

flow.context: This step of the container challenge tests the container in the dark with a torch inside.

flow.do: Ask a friend or family member to say how full it is without opening the lid.
flow.say: Can they tell how full it is, without opening the lid? Did your design work?
flow.kid: Ask someone to guess how full it is. No opening the lid! Did it work?
flow.think: Can something be both opaque and easy to check? What did you trade?
flow.context: This is the last step of the container challenge. Someone checks whether your design lets them tell how full it is.

challenges.title: The Soft Night-Light
challenges.problem: A little cousin is scared of the dark, but a bare torch is too bright and hurts their eyes. Make a shade for an LED light that lights the whole room softly, with no bright spot you can see.
constraints: Use only an LED tealight or a torch, never a flame.
From across the room, nobody should see the bright point of the light.
The light should still be bright enough to see the door.
materials: an LED tealight or small torch
butter paper, tissue, a white plastic carry bag, a steel tumbler, an old white T-shirt, a clear plastic cup
general: Put a white plastic cup or a butter-paper tube over the light. It scatters the light, so the bright point disappears.
Use more than one layer if the bright point still shows.
Point the light at a white wall and let the wall glow.
creative: Put the light inside a steel tumbler pointing up, with butter paper over the top. The tumbler sends light up and the paper spreads it.
Cut star holes in dark card wrapped around a butter-paper tube, for a night sky on the ceiling.
Stand the light behind a water-filled clear bottle with a little milk stirred in. The milk drops scatter the light into a soft glow.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own shade. Test it from across the room in the dark. Can you see the bright point? Can you see the door?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You must use translucent materials to make a soft night-light, with no bright point that hurts the eyes.

setup.art: An LED tealight glowing alone on a shelf in a dark room, with a harsh bright point.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the bare LED from across a dark room.

setup.art: The same LED covered with a tube of butter paper, now glowing softly all over.
setup.caption: 2. Try covers of different translucent materials.

setup.art: A child in bed across the room, seeing a soft glow and the outline of the door.
setup.caption: 3. Test from across the room: no bright point, but you can see the door.

flow.do: In a dark room, put the bare LED on a shelf. Stand across the room and look.
flow.say: Can you see the bright point of the light? Does it hurt to look at?
flow.kid: Look at the bare light from across the dark room. Is it too bright?
flow.context: This is the first step of the night-light challenge. You see why a bare light can be too harsh.

flow.do: 1. Your child tries covering the LED with each material. 2. For each one, they check from across the room. 3. They pick the best and improve it.
flow.say: Try each material over the light. Which hides the bright point but still lights the room?
flow.kid: Try each cover. Check from across the room. Which hides the bright point?

check.q: Which cover will best hide the bright point but still let light out?
options: A steel tumbler over the light
check.why: Butter paper is translucent. It lets light through but scatters it, so the bright point vanishes into a soft glow. A clear cup is transparent, so you still see the point. A steel tumbler over the light is opaque, so almost no light gets out.

flow.context: This step of the night-light challenge tests different covers for the light.

flow.do: Build the final shade and test it in the dark.
flow.say: Can you see the door? Can you see the bright point?
flow.kid: Build your best shade. Test it in the dark. Can you see the door?
flow.context: This step of the night-light challenge builds and tests the final shade.

flow.do: Give the night-light to someone who might like it.
flow.say: Who would like this night-light? What would you change next time?
flow.kid: Who could use your night-light? What would you change next time?
flow.think: Why are so many lampshades made of translucent materials?
flow.context: This is the last step of the night-light challenge. You share your night-light and think about what to improve.

items.p: A material that lets light straight through, so you can see clearly through it, is called…
items.why: Transparent materials let light straight through, like window glass. Picking translucent usually means mixing up 'lets light through' with 'lets a clear picture through'. Translucent things let light through but blur the picture.

items.p: Butter paper lets light through, but you cannot see clearly through it. Butter paper is…
items.why: Light gets through, but the picture is jumbled. That is translucent. Picking opaque usually means noticing that you can't see through it, but forgetting that light still comes through.

items.p: Which of these is opaque?
items.why: No light gets through a steel plate, so it is opaque. Cling film is transparent. A frosted window is translucent, because light comes in but no picture.

items.p: Sort these into transparent, translucent and opaque.
items.why: Glass and water let light straight through. Butter paper and thin cloth let light through but jumble it. Wood and brick let no light through.

items.p: A dark patch where light has been blocked is called a ____.
items.why: When an opaque thing blocks light, it leaves a dark patch behind it. That is a shadow.

items.p: Transparent things are invisible.
items.why: False. You can still see a glass of water. A little light bounces off its surfaces, and its edges bend some light.

items.p: An opaque thing makes a darker shadow than a translucent thing.
items.why: True. An opaque thing blocks all the light, so its shadow is dark. A translucent thing lets some light through, so its shadow is pale.

items.p: Match each job to the kind of material it needs.
pairs: A shop window to show sweets
A curtain for an afternoon nap
items.why: We need to see through a shop window. A bathroom needs light without a view in. A nap needs darkness. A lampshade spreads light softly.

items.p: In the gap test, you lift a material off a card of big letters. The cling film could be lifted 30 cm and the tissue only 1 cm before the word blurred. Which is more see-through?
items.why: The cling film let the word stay clear much further away, so it jumbles light less. Picking the tissue usually means reading the number as 'how much blur' instead of 'how far the picture survived'.

items.p: In the gap test, why did we rest our chin on a stack of books?
opts: To keep our eyes at the same height every time
To see better in the dark
items.why: Resting the chin keeps the eyes at the same height, so only the material changes. That makes it a fair test. If our eyes moved, the results would change for a reason that has nothing to do with the material.

items.p: Why do many bathrooms have frosted glass windows, not clear ones?
items.a: Frosted glass is translucent. It lets daylight into the bathroom. But it jumbles the light, so nobody outside can see in.
items.why: A good answer says both things: light comes in, and the picture is lost, so it is private.

items.p: Draw a torch shining on clear glass, butter paper and a wooden board. Draw what you would see on the wall behind each one.
items.a: Behind the glass, a bright clear patch. Behind the butter paper, a soft pale glow. Behind the wood, a dark shadow.
items.why: Transparent things let the light straight through. Translucent things spread it out. Opaque things block it.
items.art: A torch on the left, three empty boxes for materials, and a blank wall on the right.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? Window glass, cling film, a steel spoon, clean water.
items.why: A steel spoon is opaque. The others are all transparent.

items.p: Why do we test each material 3 times in the gap test?
opts: Because one try can be a fluke
items.why: One try can be a fluke. Our hand might wobble, or we might shout 'stop' too late. Three tries and the middle value give a fairer answer.

items.p: Sunglasses are ____. They let only part of the light through.
items.why: Tinted means darkened but still see-through. Sunglasses let some light through, so we can still see, but less of it.

items.p: It is safe to look at the Sun if you wear sunglasses.
items.why: False. Sunglasses do not make it safe to look at the Sun. Never look straight at the Sun, with or without sunglasses.

items.p: In the oil spot experiment, you put drops of water and oil on paper. Why did the oil spot become see-through?
opts: Oil is a kind of glass
The oil filled the air gaps between the paper threads
The oil made the paper thinner
items.why: Paper is a tangle of threads with air between them. Light bounces at every thread-and-air edge. Oil fills the gaps, so there are far fewer bouncing edges. Picking 'thinner' is a fair guess, but the paper is just as thick.

items.p: In the oil spot experiment, after one hour the water spot went white again, but the oil spot stayed see-through. Why?
opts: The water dried away and air filled the gaps again
items.why: Water dries up into the air. Then air fills the gaps again and the light bounces about once more. Oil does not dry away like that.

items.p: A pile of sugar is white, but sugar stirred into water is clear. Why?
opts: Light bounces off every grain's edges in the pile, but dissolved sugar is too tiny to bounce light
items.why: Many tiny edges make things look white. Dissolved sugar is split into molecules far too small to bounce light. Taste the water: the sugar is still there. Picking 'gone' forgets the sweet taste.

items.p: Clear ice is crushed into small bits. What colour does the crushed ice look?
items.why: Each little bit of ice has edges where light bounces. Lots of bits make the heap look white. That is also why snow is white.

items.p: A thin curtain hides you in the daytime, but at night with the light on inside, people outside can see you.
items.why: True. You can see from the dim side into the bright side. At night your lit room is the bright side.

items.p: In the sunglasses lab, a child could read row 5 outside with sunglasses, but only row 2 indoors with them. Why?
opts: Sunglasses only work outside because of the wind
Sunglasses let only part of the light through, and indoors there is little light to start with
items.why: Sunglasses cut the light. That helps in bright sun, but indoors there isn't much light, so cutting it makes reading harder. The chart was the same, so the letters did not change.

items.p: Which label tells you sunglasses block ultraviolet light?
items.why: Ultraviolet protection must be on the label. Darkness alone does not mean the lenses block ultraviolet light.

items.p: Why are some medicine bottles brown or opaque, and not clear?
items.a: Light can spoil some medicines. A brown or opaque bottle keeps most of that light out, so the medicine lasts longer.
items.why: Opaque and dark materials stop light reaching what is inside.

items.p: Put these in order, from MOST see-through to LEAST: butter paper, a wooden board, cling film, a cotton handkerchief.
items.why: Cling film is transparent. A loose cotton handkerchief lets light and some shapes through its gaps. Butter paper blurs the picture more. Wood is opaque. Your own order may differ a little for the cloth and the paper, depending on how thick they are.

items.p: Match each thing to why it looks white or cloudy.
pairs: The middle of an ice cube
items.why: All of these are made of clear stuff. They look white because light bounces off many tiny edges.

items.p: Your fingers glow red when you press a torch under them in the dark. Is your hand opaque or translucent? Explain.
items.a: My hand is a little translucent. Some red light gets through it, but no picture comes through. For most light it acts nearly opaque.
items.why: Any honest answer that uses what you saw is good. A hand lets a little red light through, so it is not completely opaque.

items.p: In the Three-Light Lantern, which side made a pattern of bright spots on the wall?
opts: The card jaali side with holes
items.why: The card is opaque, so it blocks light. The holes let light through, making spots in the same pattern. That is how a stone jaali makes patterns of light on the floor.

items.p: To scatter light means to send it bouncing off in many ____.
items.why: Translucent things scatter light, sending it off in many directions. That is why the picture is lost.

items.p: Draw a window with a thin curtain, once in the day and once at night with a lamp on inside. Show who can see whom.
items.a: Day: a person inside can see the street, but the street sees only a bright curtain. Night: the street can see the person's shape, but the person sees only the curtain.
items.why: Whoever is on the bright side shows up to whoever is on the dark side.
items.art: Two blank window frames side by side, labelled DAY and NIGHT.

items.p: Wet paper is usually more see-through than dry paper.
items.why: True. Water fills the air gaps between the paper threads, so light bounces less.

items.p: Why is glass see-through, but a steel plate is not?
opts: Glass's electrons can't soak up the light we see, but metal has loose electrons that catch it
items.why: In glass, the light we see doesn't have the right energy for the electrons to soak it up, so it passes by. Metals have loose electrons that catch light and send it back. Picking 'holes' is a common guess, but glass has no holes you could see through.

items.p: Window glass lets the light we see through. What does it block much of?
items.why: Window glass stops much of the Sun's ultraviolet light, the kind that causes sunburn. That is why you rarely get sunburnt through a closed window.

items.p: A brick wall is opaque to light. What can still go through it?
items.why: Radio waves are a kind of light we cannot see. They pass through brick. That is why your phone works indoors. So 'opaque' depends on the kind of light.

items.p: A sleeping glass frog becomes more see-through. How?
opts: It hides most of its red blood cells in its liver
items.why: Scientists found this in 2022. Red blood is easy to spot, so the frog packs most of its red blood cells into its liver while it sleeps. When it wakes, the blood flows out again.

items.p: For about the first 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe was…
items.why: The early universe was hot and full of loose particles that light kept bumping into, like light in fog. When it cooled and atoms formed, it became transparent. Picking 'dark and empty' is a natural guess, but it was actually glowing hot.

items.p: Old church windows are thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows downwards.
items.why: False. Old glass was made unevenly, and builders often put the thick edge at the bottom. Some old panes have the thick edge at the top. Glass at room temperature would take longer than the age of the universe to sag noticeably.

items.p: Light from the centre of the Sun travels straight out to the surface in a few seconds.
items.why: False. The Sun's inside is so crowded that light keeps bumping and changing direction. Estimates for how long it takes range from about 10,000 to 170,000 years.

items.p: Dark matter does not give out light and does not block it. How do scientists know it is there at all?
items.a: Stars and galaxies move as if something unseen is pulling on them. Vera Rubin measured how fast stars go round in galaxies, and they were too fast for the stuff we can see.
items.why: We can't see dark matter, but we can see its pull on things we can see.

items.p: Some people say good governments and companies should be 'transparent'. What do you think this means? Is it a good idea?
items.a: It means letting people see what they are doing and why, like seeing through glass. Many people think it helps stop unfairness, but some things, like your health, should stay private.
items.why: This is an open question. Any answer that explains the link to see-through materials and gives a reason is good.

items.p: Katharine Burr Blodgett invented a coating in 1938 that made glass…
opts: Even clearer, by stopping most light bouncing off it
items.why: Ordinary glass bounces back a little light at each surface. Her thin coating stopped most of that bounce, so more light went through. It is used on camera lenses and spectacles today.

items.p: Gold beaten so thin that it is called gold leaf lets a little greenish light through. What does this show?
opts: Gold is not really a metal
Even opaque materials let some light through if they are thin enough
items.why: Thickness matters. A gold coin is opaque, but gold leaf is so thin that a little light gets through. Most opaque things become translucent if made thin enough.

items.p: Sort these into: we want it transparent, or we want it opaque.
items: the front of a fish tank
items.why: We want to see clearly through lenses, fish tanks and windscreens. We want to keep light out of film, milk and a bedroom for sleep.

items.p: In the gap test, butter paper let you read the word when it touched the card, but not when lifted 2 cm. Explain why.
items.a: Butter paper scatters light a little. When it touches the card, the light from each letter has no room to spread before it gets through. Lifted up, the scattered light spreads out over a wider area, and the letters blur together.
items.why: The further the light travels after being scattered, the more it spreads. That is why tracing paper works only when it lies flat on a picture.

items.p: Why might a bird fly into a clean glass window?
opts: The glass is transparent, so the bird sees the trees behind it and not the glass
The glass is opaque to birds
items.why: Clean glass lets most light straight through, so the bird sees the view behind it. Some people stick patterns on windows so birds can see the glass.

items.p: Scientists still argue about what glass really is: a strange solid, or something in between a solid and a liquid.
items.why: True. Glass's atoms are jumbled like a liquid's, but it is stiff like a solid. How it becomes stiff as it cools is still being studied.

items.p: Invent a new use for a material that is transparent to one kind of light but opaque to another.
items.a: Any good idea. For example: a window that lets in light but blocks the heat, so rooms stay cool in summer.
items.why: Real engineers make glass like this. Any idea with a clear reason is a good answer.

quiz.why: You can see clearly through clean glass, so it is transparent. Picking butter paper usually means noticing light gets through, but forgetting the picture is blurred.
Light comes through, but no clear picture. That is translucent. Picking opaque means forgetting that the bathroom is still bright.

quiz.p: In the gap test, you lift each material off a card of big letters. What do we change, to keep it fair?
quiz.why: In a fair test we change only one thing. Here it is the material. If we changed the card or the light too, we wouldn't know which change made the difference.

quiz.p: In the gap test, the plastic bag could be lifted 6 cm before the word blurred, and the butter paper only 2 cm. How many times higher was the plastic bag?
quiz.why: 6 divided by 2 is 3. So the plastic bag could be lifted 3 times as high. Picking 4 usually means subtracting, 6 take away 2, instead of dividing.

quiz.p: Why does a drop of oil make paper see-through?
opts: Oil fills the air gaps, so light bounces less
Oil burns a hole in the paper
Oil is a kind of light
quiz.why: Light bounces at every edge between paper and air. Oil fills those gaps, so the light passes through with less bouncing.

quiz.p: Snow is made of clear ice. Why does it look white?
opts: Light bounces off millions of tiny ice crystal edges
quiz.why: Lots of tiny edges bounce light in every direction, so snow looks white. A single big clear ice cube is see-through.

quiz.p: You want your bedroom dark for an afternoon nap. Which curtain is best?
quiz.why: An opaque curtain blocks the light. Muslin is translucent, so light still comes through. A clear sheet lets almost all light in.

opts: Let part of the light through and block ultraviolet light
Make it safe to look at the Sun
quiz.why: Good sunglasses cut bright light and block ultraviolet light, which is shown by a UV400 label. They never make it safe to look at the Sun. Darker is not always safer.

quiz.p: At night, with your room lamp on, people in the street can see you through a thin curtain. Why?
opts: Your room is now the bright side
The street lights make the curtain disappear
quiz.why: Through a thin curtain, you see from the dim side into the bright side. At night your room is the bright side, so you show.

quiz.p: Your fingers glow red over a torch. What does this show?
opts: Some light can pass through your hand
quiz.why: A little light, mostly red, passes through skin and blood. So even a hand is not completely opaque. Picking 'makes red light' is a natural guess, but the glow stops when the torch is off.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about?
opts: What glass really is, deep down
quiz.why: Everyone agrees glass is transparent. But scientists still argue about what kind of stuff glass is, a stiff solid with jumbled atoms like a liquid.

quiz.p: For about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, light could not travel far through the universe. Why?
opts: The universe was full of loose particles, like a thick fog
The universe was made of glass
quiz.why: Light kept bumping into loose particles, as in fog. When it cooled and atoms formed, the universe became transparent.

applications: Windows of glass let in light and a view, while keeping out wind, rain and dust.
Frosted and patterned glass in bathrooms and office doors lets light in but keeps privacy.
Thin curtains soften bright sun. Thick blackout curtains make rooms dark for sleep.
Sunglasses cut glare and block ultraviolet light. Welders wear very dark glass to protect their eyes from the bright welding flame.
Opaque and brown bottles protect medicines, milk and cooking oil from light that spoils them.
Lampshades, kandils and paper lanterns use translucent materials to spread light softly.
Greenhouses use transparent or translucent covers so plants get light and stay warm.
Spectacles, camera lenses and phone screens need very transparent glass or plastic.
Stone jaalis in Indian buildings let in light and air but keep rooms cool and private.
Shadow-puppet artists, such as tholu bommalata puppeteers in Andhra Pradesh, use translucent painted leather so the audience sees coloured shadows.
Tracing paper and butter paper let you copy a picture by laying the paper on top.
Optical fibres of very clear glass carry internet signals as light under the oceans.
Scientists slice rocks so thin that light passes through, to study what they are made of.
Food packets for chips and biscuits are opaque, often lined with metal foil, to keep light and air out.

open_questions.why_open: Its atoms are jumbled like a liquid's, but it is stiff like a solid. How a liquid becomes glass as it cools is still one of the big puzzles of physics.

open_questions.q: What is dark matter, the stuff that light passes straight through?
open_questions.why_open: It pulls on stars and galaxies, so we know something is there. But big experiments have not yet caught a single particle of it.

open_questions.q: How does a glass frog keep its blood from clotting when it packs it into its liver?
open_questions.why_open: In people, packed blood would clot dangerously. The frog does this every night and wakes up fine. Scientists are still studying how.

open_questions.q: When a packet of light reaches a window, what decides whether it goes through or bounces back?
open_questions.why_open: Only the share can be predicted. Most physicists say each packet is pure chance. Some think hidden details might decide. Experiments have not settled what this chance really is.

open_questions.q: Exactly how long does light take to escape from the middle of the Sun?
open_questions.why_open: Estimates range from about 10,000 to 170,000 years, because it depends on details of the Sun's inside that we cannot measure directly.

open_questions.q: Could we make walls, cars or even bones that are see-through, but strong?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have made see-through wood and see-through ceramics. Making them cheap and strong enough for everyday use is still being worked on.

maths.problem: In the gap test, the plastic bag could be lifted 6 cm before the word blurred. The butter paper could be lifted only 2 cm. How many times higher was the plastic bag?
maths.explain: The plastic bag could be lifted to 6 cm. The butter paper only to 2 cm. 6 divided by 2 is 3. So the plastic bag went 3 times as high. You can check: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.
maths.context: This is about the gap test. You lay a material on a card of big letters and lift it slowly. You measure how high it goes before the word blurs. Higher means more see-through.
maths.why_maths: Scientists don't just say 'the bag is more see-through'. They ask 'how much more?' Dividing tells us: this many times.

maths.problem: In the gap test, the handkerchief's three tries were 4 cm, 2 cm and 3 cm. What is the middle value?
maths.explain: Put the three numbers in order: 2, 3, 4. The middle one is 3. So the middle value is 3 cm.
maths.context: This is about the gap test, where you test each material 3 times and take the middle value. You lift each material off a card of letters and measure when the word blurs.
maths.why_maths: One try can be a fluke. Putting three tries in order and taking the middle one gives a fairer answer.

maths.problem: In the oil spot experiment, each spot gets a score from 0 to 3. The dry spot scored 1, the water spot scored 2, and the oil spot scored 3. After one hour, the water spot scored 1. By how much did the water spot's score drop?
maths.explain: The water spot first scored 2. After an hour it scored 1. 2 take away 1 is 1. So it dropped by 1, back to the same as the dry spot.
maths.context: This is about the oil spot experiment. You put drops of water and oil on paper, and score how see-through each spot is from 0, no light, to 3, words you can read.

chart.title: See-through score straight away and after one hour

maths.why_maths: Taking one score from another shows how much something changed. Here it shows the water drying away.

maths.problem: The Three-Light Lantern has 4 side windows. One is clear plastic, two are butter paper, and one is a card jaali. What fraction of the windows are butter paper?
maths.answer: Two quarters, which is the same as one half.
maths.explain: There are 4 windows. 2 of them are butter paper. So 2 out of 4 are butter paper. That is two quarters. Two quarters is the same as one half.
maths.context: This is about the lantern project, where you build a box lantern with a different material on each of its 4 sides and light it with an LED.
maths.why_maths: Fractions tell us what part of the whole is made of each material. That helps you plan how much of each to cut.

maths.problem: Sunglasses with a dark tint let through about 1 out of every 5 parts of the light. If 100 bits of light hit the lenses, about how many get through?
maths.explain: 1 out of every 5 gets through. 100 is 20 groups of 5. One from each group is 20. So about 20 bits of light get through, and about 80 are stopped.
maths.context: This is about the sunglasses lab, where you read a letter chart with and without sunglasses. Sunglasses are tinted, so they let only part of the light through.
maths.why_maths: Sharing into equal groups shows how much light the lenses really let through. That explains why the letters are hard to read in a dim room.

roots.context: We have been learning how light goes through some things, gets jumbled in others, and is stopped by the rest. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: See-through or solid is not something a thing has by itself. It is a meeting between the thing and the light.
deep_truth.habit: We put labels on things, like 'transparent' or 'opaque', as if they were fixed forever. But the same butter paper is clear when it touches the page and cloudy when lifted. Your 'solid' hand lets red light through. A brick wall lets radio waves pass. The label belongs to the meeting, not just the thing.
deep_truth.evidence: In this unit, oil turned paper see-through, crushing turned clear ice white, and a curtain hid Meenu by day but showed her at night.

three.who_am_i: You look solid, yet light passes through your fingers. You are more open than you look.
three.what_is_life: Some living things hide by being see-through, like the glass frog. Life plays with light.
three.what_is_this_world: The whole universe was once a fog. Then it cleared, and light could travel. We still see that first clear light today.

roots.thread: DeepKids believes everything rises from one ground, and shows up as many things. Light is one of the ways the many things meet. A window, a curtain and a wall are not three separate kinds of thing. They are the same light meeting different arrangements of atoms. What we call clear, cloudy or blocked is the One, meeting itself in different ways.

teachings.teaching: A father, Uddalaka, asks his son to put salt in water overnight. In the morning the son cannot see the salt. But every sip tastes salty. The father says: in the same way, what is finest is everywhere, unseen. 'You are that.'
teachings.link: Sugar stirred into water becomes clear and invisible, but it is still there in every sip. Not seeing something does not mean it is not there.

teachings.teaching: The face of truth is covered by a golden lid. The seeker asks for the lid to be taken away, so the truth can be seen.
teachings.link: Some coverings are opaque and hide what is behind them. Meenu's quilt hid the light. The verse asks what is covering what we really are.

teachings.teaching: For now we see through a glass, darkly. Paul, the writer, means we see things only dimly, as if through cloudy glass, and one day we may see clearly.
teachings.link: Glass in Paul's time was often cloudy and translucent. He uses it to say that what we know now is only a blurry picture.

science.text: Whether a material is see-through depends on its thickness, its tiny edges and the kind of light. Nothing is see-through or blocking for every kind of light.
For about 380,000 years, the young universe was opaque, like fog. Then it became transparent, and that first light still reaches us.

other_view.who: The Charvaka thinkers of ancient India, and many scientists today
other_view.view: Transparency is just atoms and light, and nothing more. There is no deeper One behind it. Light passes through glass because of electrons and energy, and that is the whole story. This is an honest view, and many careful people hold it.

practice.title: Look at, then look through
practice.say: Let's stand at a window together. First, look at the glass. Can you find a speck of dust, or a smudge? Now, let your eyes go through the glass, to the farthest thing you can see. Breathe slowly three times. Did you notice the glass disappear? It was there the whole time. Now hold your hand up to the light, and look at the soft glow at the edges of your fingers. Where does your hand stop, and the light begin?
practice.kid: Stand at a window. Look at the glass. Find a smudge. Now look through it, far away. Breathe slowly three times. Where did the glass go?

ask: Is anything really see-through, or does it depend on the light?
What things in your life are like a thin curtain, hiding some things and showing others?
Is the sugar in the water still sugar, if you can't see it?
What might be all around us, like dark matter, that we cannot see at all?
roots.art: A child at a window, half the glass showing a smudge in sharp focus, half fading away to show a far-off tree, with soft light glowing at the edges of the child's raised hand.
